w: Built in 1894 as pure experiment, this vessel became the fastest ship afloat and proved it at the 1897 Spithead Navy Review, outrunning the fleet. Turbine power was standard across steamships within years. She's dry-docked at the Discovery Museum now -- her engine shipped south to London's Science Museum.
s: The first turbine ship, briefly the world's fastest
_facts: First steam turbine-powered steamship, built 1894 by Charles Algernon Parsons
Easily the fastest ship in the world at the time
Demonstrated dramatically at the 1897 Spithead Navy Review, setting the standard for the next generation of steamships
Now at the Discovery Museum, Newcastle; original powerplant at the Science Museum, London

w: The world's first tilting bridge, and it pivots slowly enough to watch, letting river traffic pass beneath. Opened in 2001 to link Gateshead's arts quarter with Newcastle's Quayside, the shape earned it a nickname -- the Blinking Eye, or the Winking Eye, depending who's telling it.
s: The world's first tilting bridge, the 'Blinking Eye'
_facts: First tilting bridge ever constructed; opened 2001
Pedestrian and cyclist bridge linking Gateshead arts quarter with Newcastle's Quayside
Nicknamed the 'Blinking Eye' or 'Winking Eye' Bridge for its shape and tilting method

w: The castle that gave Newcastle its name -- literally. Robert Curthose, the Conqueror's eldest son, built a wooden fort here in 1080 fresh from fighting the Scots, and called it the 'New Castle.' Henry II rebuilt it in stone; Henry III added the Black Gate. The railway now runs through the 75-foot gap between the two.
s: The castle that gave Newcastle its name
_facts: Built on the site of a Roman fort and settlement, Pons Aelius, guarding a Tyne bridge
Robert Curthose (William the Conqueror's eldest son) built a wooden motte-and-bailey castle here in 1080, the 'New Castle upon Tyne'
Henry II built the stone Castle Keep 1172-1177; Henry III added the Black Gate 1247-1250
A 75-foot gap between the Keep and the Black Gate is almost entirely filled by the railway

w: The easternmost fort on Hadrian's Wall, garrisoned for close to 300 years guarding the point where the Wall met the Tyne. Modern Wallsend grew up on top of it, but Segedunum is now the most thoroughly excavated fort along the whole Wall, its baths and foundations laid bare as part of the World Heritage Site.
s: Hadrian's Wall's most fully excavated Roman fort
_facts: Roman fort at the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, near the River Tyne at Wallsend
In use for around 300 years, roughly 122 to 400 AD
The most thoroughly excavated fort along the whole of Hadrian's Wall
Part of the Hadrian's Wall UNESCO World Heritage Site
